entry: Air burst explosion over remote [[Siberia]], Russia, in 1908. On the morning of June 30, 1908, a blast in the [[Taiga|taiga]] flattened nearly 2,150 km² (830 sq mi) of forest, knocked witnesses to the ground, and shattered windows within 200 km (120 mi). Seismic stations recorded a magnitude close to 5 on the [[Richter scale]]. The scientific consensus attributes it to a [[Meteoroid|meteoroid]] 50–60 m (160–200 ft) in diameter that exploded at an altitude of 5–10 km (3.1–6.2 mi), although no fragment has been identified. It is the most violent impact event on Earth recorded in modern times.

Capital and largest city of [[Tunisia]], on the Gulf of Tunis in North Africa. As of 2020 it was the third-largest city in the [[Maghreb]] region, after Casablanca and Algiers, and the fifteenth-largest in the [[Arab world]]. The city extends along the coastal plain and surrounding hills, behind the Lake of Tunis and the port of La Goulette. At its core lies the Medina, a [[World Heritage Site]]. East of the Medina, through the Sea Gate, begins the modern Ville Nouvelle, traversed by the grand Avenue Habib Bourguiba, where colonial-era buildings contrast with older structures. Suburbs to the east by the sea include [[Carthage]], La Marsa and Sidi Bou Said. Settlements in the area are attested from the 4th century BC, and it was one of the first towns in the region to fall under Carthaginian control. Tunis is the focus of Tunisian political and administrative life.

Republic in the [[Maghreb]] region of North Africa, with Tunis as its capital. It is bordered by [[Algeria]] to the west and southwest, [[Libya]] to the southeast and the [[Mediterranean Sea]] to the north and east. [[Carthage]], the most powerful Phoenician settlement by the 7th century BC, was a mercantile empire and military rival to the Roman Republic until 146 BC, when Rome defeated it and occupied Tunisia for most of the next 800 years. Arab Muslims conquered the country in the 7th century AD, bringing [[Islam]] and Arab culture, and by about the 15th century the region was almost completely Arabized. The [[Ottoman Empire]] held control from 1546 until 1881, when France conquered Tunisia, and independence came in 1956. The 2011 Tunisian Revolution ended the 24-year rule of Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and sparked the broader [[Arab Spring]].

Malaysian statesman, first prime minister of [[Malaysia]] (1957–70). A prince of the Kedah Sultanate, he graduated from St Catharine's College, [[Cambridge]], then joined the colonial [[Civil service|civil service]] and became a public prosecutor in 1949. He became president of UMNO in 1951 and formed the Alliance Party in 1952. After the Alliance won a landslide in the 1955 general election, he became chief minister of the Federation of Malaya. He secured independence for Malaya through the Treaty of London in 1956 and proclaimed it in 1957. In 1965, after mutual provocations with the People's Action Party led by [[Lee Kuan Yew]], he resolved to expel [[Singapore]] from the federation. He stepped down in 1970 after violent unrest during the 13 May incident, and was succeeded by Abdul Razak Hussein.

Underground or undersea passageway, dug through soil or rock or laid under water. It is usually enclosed except for a portal at each end, and may carry road or foot traffic, trains, or a canal. Some tunnels serve as sewers or [[Aqueduct (water supply)|aqueducts]], and utility tunnels carry steam, power or telecommunication cables. The central portions of a [[Rapid transit|rapid transit]] network are usually in tunnels. The first artificial tunnel is believed to have been built in [[Babylon]] around 2200 BC, joining a temple to a palace by the cut-and-cover technique. The Siloam Tunnel in [[Jerusalem]], built around the 8th century BC, was the earliest known tunnel excavated from both ends. Secret tunnels serve military purposes or smuggling of weapons, contraband, or people, and early tunneling evolved from [[Mining|mining]] and [[Military engineering|military engineering]].

Museum in [[Phnom Penh]], Cambodia, documenting the [[Cambodian genocide]]. The former secondary school became Security Prison 21 (S-21), run by the [[Khmer Rouge]] from 1975 to 1979. It was one of between 150 and 196 torture and execution centers established by the Khmer Rouge and their secret police, and an estimated 20,000 people were imprisoned there from 1976 to 1979. Prisoners were repeatedly tortured. Vietnamese forces uncovered the prison in 1979. In 2010 the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia convicted its chief, Kang Kek Iew, of crimes against humanity.

American rapper and actor, also known as 2Pac and Makaveli. Born in [[New York City]] to parents who were members of the [[Black Panther Party]], he moved to the [[San Francisco Bay Area]] in 1988. His debut album, *2Pacalypse Now* (1991), established him as a central figure in West Coast [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]]. His Diamond-certified album *All Eyez on Me* (1996), the first hip-hop double album, yielded two Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles, "California Love" and "How Do U Want It". In 1994 he was shot five times in the lobby of a New York recording studio and served eight months in prison on sexual abuse charges. He was killed in a drive-by shooting in Paradise, Nevada, and in 2026 a Compton Crips member, Duane Davis, was convicted of orchestrating the killing. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him among the 100 Greatest Artists of All Time.

Soviet and Russian medium-range trijet airliner, designed in the mid-1960s. Known to NATO as "Careless," it carried half of all Aeroflot passengers, about 137.5 million a year in 1990, and remained the standard domestic airliner of Russia and former Soviet states until the mid-2000s. It was exported to 17 non-Russian airlines and used as a head-of-state transport by several [[Air force|air forces]]. With a cruising speed of 850 km/h (460 kn; 530 mph) and a range of 5,280 km (3,280 mi), it operated from unpaved airfields in the [[Arctic]] regions of northern and eastern Russia, where other airliners could not fly.

Family of medium-sized, brightly colored [[Bird|birds]] endemic to [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]]. The family, Musophagidae, also includes plantain-eaters and go-away-birds; the turacos are noted for pigments giving their feathers bright green and red colors. Turacoverdin is the only true green pigment in birds, and the red pigment turacin differs from the [[Carotenoid|carotenoid]] reds of other birds. Traditionally grouped with the [[Cuckoo|cuckoos]], turacos are now usually placed in their own order, Musophagiformes. All species are frugivorous, also eating leaves, buds and flowers, and [[Fig|figs]] are an important part of their diet. They are gregarious, non-migratory birds that move in family groups of up to 10. Many species are noisy, and the go-away-birds take their common name from their alarm calls. They build large stick nests in trees and lay 2 or 3 eggs.

Rotary mechanical device that extracts [[Energy|energy]] from a fluid flow and converts it into useful [[Work (physics)|work]]. The work may drive a generator to produce electricity. A turbine is a turbomachine with at least one moving part. Its moving part, the rotor assembly, is a shaft or drum with attached blades; the fluid acts on the blades to impart rotational energy. Gas, steam and water turbines have a casing that contains and controls the working fluid. [[Impulse (physics)|Impulse]] turbines change the direction of a high-velocity fluid jet, while reaction turbines develop [[Torque|torque]] by reacting to pressure changes in the fluid. The word *turbine* was first applied to the device in 1822 by French mining engineer Claude Burdin, from Latin *turbo*, meaning vortex. [[Hero of Alexandria]] demonstrated the principle with an aeolipile in the first century AD, and early examples include [[Windmill|windmills]] and waterwheels. Modern [[Steam turbine|steam turbines]] often combine reaction and impulse designs.

Type of airbreathing [[Jet engine|jet engine]] in which a ducted fan, driven by a gas [[Turbine|turbine]], forces air rearward. Unlike a turbojet, part of the air entering the engine bypasses the core, combustion chamber and turbines. Most commercial airliners use high-bypass designs, which produce most of their thrust from a large mass of low-speed bypass air. Most modern fighter engines are low-bypass designs, which often use afterburners. Frank Whittle described the principle in a March 1936 patent. Turbofans power aircraft such as the [[Boeing 747]] and [[Airbus A300]].

Large species of [[Flatfish|flatfish]], *Scophthalmus maximus*, in the family Scophthalmidae. It is a demersal fish native to marine or [[Brackish water|brackish]] waters of the northeast [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]], the [[Baltic Sea]] and the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. It feeds on bottom-dwelling prey such as sand eels and gobies. It is an important food fish with bright white flesh that stays white when cooked, and it yields four fillets. Turbot is farmed in Bulgaria, Canada, France, Spain, Portugal, Romania, Turkey, Chile, Norway and China. [[Black Sea]] turbot, or kalkan, were once included in this species but are now regarded as separate. True turbot are not found in the Northwest Atlantic, where the name applies to the Greenland halibut.

Fluid motion characterized by chaotic changes in [[Pressure|pressure]] and flow velocity. It contrasts with laminar flow, in which fluid moves in parallel layers with no disruption between them. Most fluid flows in nature and engineering are turbulent, as with surf, fast-flowing rivers and chimney smoke. Turbulence arises when excess [[Kinetic energy|kinetic energy]] overcomes the damping effect of [[Viscosity|viscosity]], producing unsteady vortices that increase [[Drag (physics)|drag]] due to friction. The onset of turbulence can be predicted by the dimensionless [[Reynolds number]], the ratio of kinetic energy to viscous damping, yet turbulence has long resisted detailed physical analysis. Physicist [[Richard Feynman]] described turbulence as the most important unsolved problem in classical physics. Most of the terrestrial [[Atmospheric circulation|atmospheric circulation]] is turbulent. Its intensity affects fish ecology, air pollution, precipitation and climate change.

Capital and largest city of [[Piedmont]], northern Italy (pop., 2026: 855,654). It lies on the western bank of the Po River, near the western Alpine arch, and was the first capital of the [[Kingdom of Italy]] from 1861 to 1865. From 1563 it was capital of the Duchy of Savoy, and it was the political center of the Risorgimento that led to [[Unification of Italy]]. It was also the birthplace of [[Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour]]. Postwar Turin became a major industrial center, part of an industrial triangle with Milan and Genoa, and is home to much of Italy's automotive industry, including the headquarters of Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo. The city is known for its Baroque, Rococo and [[Art Nouveau]] architecture, and for the Mole Antonelliana, which houses the National Museum of Cinema. It is also famous for the [[Shroud of Turin]] and the [[Association football|association football]] club Juventus.

Mathematical model of computation describing an [[Abstract machine|abstract machine]] that manipulates symbols on a strip of tape. Despite its simplicity, it can implement any [[Algorithm|algorithm]]. A head reads and writes symbols on an infinite tape, following a finite table of rules. [[Alan Turing]] invented it in 1936 and used it to prove the uncomputability of the Entscheidungsproblem, the decision problem of whether every mathematical statement is provable or disprovable. The machine's minimalist design makes it too slow for practical computation, so real computers use [[Random-access memory|random-access memory]]. Nearly all [[Programming language|programming languages]] are Turing complete if finite memory limits are ignored.

Test of a machine's ability to imitate human intelligence, devised by [[Alan Turing]]. In the modern version, a human evaluator judges a text transcript of a conversation between a human and a machine, and the machine passes if the evaluator cannot reliably tell them apart. Turing introduced it in his 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" as the imitation game. The results depend on how closely the machine's answers resemble human ones, not on their correctness. Critics such as John Searle argue that the test cannot detect [[Consciousness|consciousness]].

Genus of large, heavyset birds in the order [[Galliformes]], native to the [[Americas]]. It includes the [[Wild turkey|wild turkey]] of Southern, Central and Eastern North America and the ocellated turkey of the [[Yucatán Peninsula]] in Mexico. Males of both species have a fleshy wattle called a snood. The wild turkey is the ancestor of the [[Domestic turkey|domestic turkey]], which indigenous peoples domesticated and later carried to Eurasia in the [[Columbian exchange]]. The name originally denoted the African guineafowl, imported to Europe via Turkey, and was transferred to this bird after English colonies were established in the New World.

[[Language family]] of more than 35 documented languages spoken by the [[Turkic peoples]] of Eurasia. Spoken by some 200 million people, the languages range from the [[Balkans]] and Eastern Europe to [[Central Asia]], [[East Asia]], [[Siberia]] and West Asia. Turkish has the most speakers, with native speakers accounting for about 38% of the total, followed by Uzbek. Vowel harmony, agglutination, subject-object-verb order and the lack of grammatical gender are almost universal across the family. Most classifications divide it into two branches: Oghur, whose only surviving member is Chuvash, and Common Turkic, which includes all others. A proposed link to other families, the Altaic hypothesis, is widely rejected by historical linguists. On 15 December 1893 the Orkhon Inscriptions, among the first Turkic texts, were decrypted, and [[UNESCO]] declared December 15 "World Turkic Language Family Day".

Diverse ethnic groups of West, Central, East and North Asia and parts of Europe, who speak [[Turkic languages]]. Proto-Turkic may have originated in Central-East Asia, potentially in the Altai-Sayan region, [[Mongolia]] or Tuva. Early speakers were possibly both hunter-gatherers and farmers, and later became nomadic [[Nomad|pastoralists]]. Many groups became Turkic through language shift, [[Adoption|adoption]], conquest and [[Religious conversion|religious conversion]]. Modern groups include the Azerbaijanis, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Turkmens, Turkish people, Tuvans, [[Uyghurs]], Uzbeks and Yakuts. The earliest known use of the name Turk, for the [[Göktürks]], dates to no later than 587 AD. Beyond language, they share to varying degrees cultural traits, ancestry from a common gene pool and historical experiences.

Interwar conflict in Turkey, 1919–1923. A series of military campaigns and a revolution waged by the Turkish National Movement after the defeat of the [[Ottoman Empire]] in [[World War I]]. Turkish nationalists fought Allied and separatist forces over [[Self-determination|self-determination]] in Anatolia and eastern Thrace. [[Mustafa Kemal Atatürk]], sent by the sultan to restore order, became the leader of nationalist resistance and set up a counter-government in Ankara. The Allies agreed to send a Greek force to occupy Smyrna ([[İzmir]]), inflaming sectarian tensions. The Grand National Assembly signed the Treaty of Lausanne, more favorable to Turkey than Sèvres. The Grand National Assembly declared the Republic of Turkey on 29 October 1923, ending the Ottoman sultanate and [[Caliphate|caliphate]]. The Muslim share of the population rose from 80% to 98%, as the [[Armenian genocide]] and the Greek genocide largely destroyed the Christian presence in Anatolia.

Most widely spoken [[Turkic languages|Turkic]] language, with around 90 million speakers. It is the national language of Turkey and one of two official languages of Cyprus. In 1928, as one of Atatürk's reforms, the Ottoman Turkish alphabet was replaced with the [[Latin script|Latin-script]] alphabet. Turkish grammar is generally very regular, with subject-object-verb word order and no noun classes or grammatical gender. Vowel harmony marks its [[Phonology|phonology]]: native words typically contain only front or only back [[Vowel|vowels]]. Over 80% of its vocabulary is native Turkic, though many [[Arabic]] loanwords were replaced by Turkish coinages during language reform. It has a strong T–V distinction that marks politeness, social distance and familiarity.

Landlocked republic in [[Central Asia]], with Ashgabat as its capital. It is bordered by Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to the north, Afghanistan to the southeast, Iran to the south and southwest, and the [[Caspian Sea]] to the west. Merv, one of the oldest oasis cities in Central Asia, was once among the largest cities in the world and an important stop on the [[Silk Road]]. Annexed by the [[Russian Empire]] in 1881, it became a Soviet republic in 1925 and gained independence after the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991. It holds the world's fifth-largest [[Natural gas|natural gas]] reserves, and most of the country is covered by the [[Karakum Desert]]. Since independence it has been ruled by repressive totalitarian regimes, most recently under Serdar Berdimuhamedow, who won a 2022 presidential election that observers judged neither free nor fair. It is a member of the [[United Nations]].

[[British Overseas Territories|British Overseas Territory]] in the Lucayan Archipelago of the Atlantic Ocean, made up of the larger Caicos Islands and smaller Turks Islands. Known for tourism and as an offshore financial center, the islands were inhabited by Lucayan ([[Taíno|Taíno]]) people for centuries before the first recorded European sighting in 1512. The British Empire eventually gained control, and the islands were governed indirectly through [[Bermuda]], the Bahamas and [[Jamaica]]. When the Bahamas became independent in 1973, the islands received their own governor and have remained autonomous since. Cockburn Town on Grand Turk has been the capital since 1766.

[[Flowering plant|Flowering plant]] of the [[Ginger|ginger]] family, *Curcuma longa*. Native to the [[Indian subcontinent]] and Southeast Asia, it is used as a spice. Its rhizomes are dried and ground into a deep orange-yellow powder used as a coloring and flavoring agent in Asian cuisines, especially in [[Curry|curries]]. Although long used in [[Ayurveda|Ayurvedic]] medicine, there is no high-quality clinical evidence that turmeric or its principal constituent, curcumin, is effective for treating any disease. Curcumin is approved as a food additive by the [[World Health Organization]] and [[European Union]]. Turmeric is generally safe, though immune-mediated liver injury has rarely been linked to it.

Root vegetable, *Brassica rapa* subsp. *rapa*, commonly grown in [[Temperate climate|temperate climates]] for its white fleshy taproot. Small, tender varieties are eaten by people, while larger ones are grown as [[Livestock|livestock]] feed. The name is also used for [[Rutabaga|swede]], a different but related vegetable. Edible turnips were domesticated in [[Central Asia]] several thousand years ago, and Central Asian varieties are the most genetically diverse crops. The vegetable later spread to Europe and East Asia, and became an important food in the Hellenistic and Roman world. In antiquity, Jews regarded it as a food of the poor; the [[Talmud]] declares, "Woe to the house in which the turnip passes." It reached Japan by 700 CE.
